utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good morning to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Yes, Madam Vidovic, appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends. I am Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries? I see -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Only short to update --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Only short, to update Your Honours. Yesterday there was a question about P99, about the everyone-for-everyone exchange. It was a question regarding the analysis on handwriting. We, as a Prosecution, did, as you know, the signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- and the outcome of it, we tried to -- we tried to get the information about the possibilities, the opportunities, to do the handwriting analysis, but there is not enough material to execute that on an expert level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I am grateful -- I am grateful for that information, Mr. Wubben. Any preliminaries on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just two matters. One is that I understand that the DVD of the Telering programme which we saw yesterday is being copied by the technical people this morning. Apparently, it is a long process, and the technical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You burn one from the other. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is what we're informed by the technical people, that only recently do they have the equipment for burning DVD to DVD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's true, that's true. That I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We certainly have never had that equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, that I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's being done, and I understand the copy of the DVD will be available this morning to the Prosecution. We informed that of that yesterday. That's one matter. The second is that, due to the miracle of Amazon, I have copies of War Hospital for everyone. Perhaps this is a good moment to pass it up. I understand the Prosecution already have their copy. So I have one for the Registry and one for each of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the book we were referring to yesterday, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One goes into the file, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in effect, I'll be asking for the whole book to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the book itself, Madam Registrar. Yesterday, we said 493. What was the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I suggest is the following: That will be D198, this will be D199, because that is a bundle that you are using for the purpose of examining the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This, I take it, will be used for other purposes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, in case there are pages which I refer to which weren't in the bundle, and also generally it was just so that the extracts wouldn't be completely out of context. If need be, they can be read in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Jones referred to -- that the copy is with the Prosecution. We didn't receive a copy of the book from Defence counsel. We have to rely on library or private initiatives in that respect. When it comes to handing over of such a book to the Bench for context purposes, it should be that a copy should also be available for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour, when I said the Prosecution I understand has a copy, it's because Mr. Wubben said they had made copies of the book, so I understood that they had their own copy. I might add I bought these copies at my own personal expense, and I'm happy to buy a copy for the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It may take some time because I'll have to order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe they will have less objections today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we bring in the witness? Today, as I told you, we'll finish at 12.30, because at 1 then I start a new case, another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning from the Bench as well, Dr. Mujkanovic. We are proceeding with the cross-examination. May I just remind you that you are still testifying under oath, your duty to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One preliminary matter, Dr. Mujkanovic. I think yesterday, at the end of the session, there might have been a misinterpretation. I certainly wasn't blaming you for any delays or any interruptions. I understand that it might have been misinterpreted to suggest that I was saying the witness had caused delay, and I certainly wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you saying? I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can explain, Your Honour. At the end of yesterday's session, I said with the delays and interruptions, that we may be here for some time. I understand from my colleagues that was interpreted to suggest that it was the witness I was criticising, in the interpretation in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I certainly wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I wasn't aware. I mean, I usually follow everything, and I can assure you I don't miss a word, but I don't follow the proceedings in the original language and in the interpretation at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, that's important for you to clear up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wanted to make that absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you saw the video of the Telering programme yesterday which was on the OBN TV Telering show, aired on the 29th of April, 2004. I'd simply ask you this: Do you stand by the comments which you made on that programme about the situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in that interview, you mentioned that people actually died of starvation in the enclave as a result of the food crisis. Can you confirm that that did occur?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would simply ask that the programme -- the DVD and the transcript be given a Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Didn't we give it one yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think we didn't because I wasn't proceeding to ask any questions about it. I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can help me there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They didn't, no. So the DVD itself will be given now D200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the translation, or the transcript which we had yesterday will be given D200.1. D200.1, all right? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: A request to the Defence counsel, if he can also be specific to referring to what time frame is mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the DVD?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: The starvation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The starvation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were referring to the DVD.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think the witness understood the question and answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you tell us when starvation occurred in the enclave, if possible?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My whole statement is in relation to my stay in Srebrenica, from the 5th of August, 1992 to the 22nd of April, 1993. This is the time period that I have in mind, the period through which I stayed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it would be right to say that people were dying of starvation right throughout that period, from August 1992 through to April 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starvation peaked in December, January, and until as late as early March 1993. When the parachuting operation was launched, food parcels were dropped from planes into the Srebrenica enclave. Therefore, December and January especially were difficult months, when a great number of people, because of poor intake of rich foodstuffs, simply starved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday Eric Dachy who arrived with an aid convoy in December 1992 and again in March 1993. Did he tell you on either occasion about the difficulties he had had getting the convoys into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he even wrote me a letter. It was a well-known fact that Serbs prevented no convoys -- that Serbs allowed no convoys to enter Srebrenica, and then the first convoy was given a green light in 1992, when Eric promised that he would send more medical supplies, bandages, medicines, some equipment, things that the war hospital was in bad need of. The next convoy came in six or seven days later, in early December, and that was the last entry of any convoy until late March or early April the next year, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you understand from your conversations with him that the Serbs were obstructing food, deliberately obstructing food from entering the enclave?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my conversations with him -- rather, I should say, that was when I was introduced to him, that was when I first met him, and the Serbs then allowed for the entire convoy, including journalists and some other people, to enter the enclave. It was quite a sight at the time, because everyone could see what life was like in the enclave. They were given the right to stay for about three hours, if I remember well, inside the enclave. Eric wanted to use the time as best as he could to look at the hospital, see the way we worked there, to visit the patients. He realised that we had a problem there and he said he would try to get some medical supplies for us, such as medicines and bandages, but that he couldn't guarantee anything. He said he would remain adamant and try his best. It wasn't easy to enter Srebrenica. I can illustrate this with another example. There was a field hospital that was donated by the French government, led by Mr. Bernard Kouchner. I think it had been in Serbia for about a month, waiting to be allowed entry into Srebrenica. It was necessary also for doctors and medical supplies to join the convoy. However, this field hospital was never eventually allowed in, and it had to be sent back to France. This was a recurring problem with convoys and with medical supplies coming in. Based on all of this, it's easy to conclude that the only way for Srebrenica to get the necessary foodstuffs, the basic necessities, and in order for an institution like our hospital to function, was to drop supplies from the air. Planes would do that at night. Those were brown parcels containing meals, soldiers' meals, lunch packs, dry rations. They would drop these supplies by plane, such as basic medical supplies, some instruments, bandages, that sort of thing. That was the only way these supplies could come in. This happened before -- this was done by March, when these air drops were organised to drop the necessary food and medical supplies into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And when the air drops started, did you hear or learn that people from Srebrenica, Muslims, were killing each other over the food which was contained in these drops? Could you say yes --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I heard about several cases of people killing each other in order to get some food. There was no way to say how long this would go on for. I must say that this operation from Srebrenica was coordinated by a number of officers who came in escorting General Morillon. They stayed and he left. They were tasked with coordinating the entire operation. There were several journalists present there, too; Tony Birtley from ABC News, there was a photographer from Berlin, Philip von Recklinghausen. I knew them both well because they were both my patients. They had both been wounded seriously on two different occasions. I performed surgery on them, and then even after three days, Tony was not allowed to leave Srebrenica. It was only on the third day that he was allowed to leave for Split, and from there on to London. There was no way to tell how long these air drops would continue. It was a day longer each time they took a decision. There was a lot of confusion because people were trying to grab as much food as possible, and to have some to put aside. Sometimes people were killed as a result of these clashes. Once we found two bodies in the south sector of the Srebrenica area, in Vojna, I mean the town itself. This must have been recorded by Tony Birtley, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I could ask you to look, and Your Honours to look, at page 130 of the War Hospital, and if the witness could be shown D198, page 130. There's an extract which I'd like to read. This extract, just by way of background, describes a sight that you and Eric Dachy, from MSF, apparently saw once air drops started. Page 130, and I'll just read it into the record. It's just two paragraphs. "Eric sees fires burning and, in the light of the waning gibbous moon, makes out an unreal sight - long, black snakes wriggling slowly across the snowy white mountainside. He is spellbound. The true meaning of the image sharpens under Nedret's narration. "The snakes are lines of hungry, exhausted Srebrenica residents who struggle up the mountain, desperate for manna-like provisions falling from the sky. Awaiting supplies being airdropped by the U.S. air force, a small city's worth gather around burning car tires. Many, recently expelled from their villages by the Serb advance, have walked miles to Srebrenica only to find themselves stuck outdoors in the freezing cold with no food." So my question is, and I think you've answered it already, but do you recall witnessing that sight with Eric Dachy? I can put it a different way. Do you remember explaining to Eric Dachy what this sight was?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had been staying at the Domavija Hotel. From the balcony of my room, you had a clear view of Bojna. The distance is perhaps 1.000 metres as the crow flies. Every night people came with torches and waited for the air drops to start. You can never tell when these would begin. They usually started late in the evening, from 11.00 on. But people were already standing there, waiting. As I was watching this, I had the impression that this was a large town that I could see in the distance. I was using a jeep vehicle at the time that the Medecins sans Frontieres had given me to use. Eric asked me to get into the jeep and for us to go from the hotel to the area. He wanted to see for himself, and Tony Birtley was with us too. We took the road up the hill known as Bojna. We stayed there briefly and then drove back. I can tell you that there were thousands of people there, flailing torches, lighting fires, waiting. And then the tactics of the drops themselves changed. Sometimes -- for a while, they would drop parcels into the Bojna area, into the woods, with huge parachutes. These palettes or parcels would sometimes weigh between 800 and 900 kilogrammes, depending on what was in them. This was the reason that patients often came in to see me whose bones were smashed or crunched by these heavy parcels falling on their limbs. We launched a protest saying this was not all right. As soon as someone grabbed hold of an entire parcel, that's when they started shooting at one another, because people would fight for possession. They changed that then, and they would throw small individual parcels from the planes all over the streets and town. There was always a possibility that one of these smaller parcels would never be found. Those were rather large planes making the drops, and as they flew in the night, the sound became somehow blunt because, when they would dive was when they would begin to drop the parcels. The planes would nose-dive, and then they would start dropping the parcels over the houses and streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So they switched from large palettes to distributing I think what's called "meals ready to eat," which were then picked up?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned going with Tony Birtley, and Eric Dachy to see this sight. Did Tony Birtley film what was going on on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly when that was?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was March 1993. It was approximately March. That was the period, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you turn to page 132, there's another section dealing with this phenomenon, and I'll just read it: "While the supplies are desperately needed, spreading the staff of life has spread suffering and death, too. The first attempts at airdrops fell into areas near Serb control, and Srebrenicans fetching the supplies came under sniper fire. The airdrops have also lured soldiers from their posts, leaving front lines vulnerable to Serb attacks. Even worse, the huge palettes, although tied to parachutes, have crushed several people. The desperate have fought and killed one another over the contents. With no clear distribution system, gathering supplies is a fight of the fittest. "Eric --" and that's Eric Dachy -- "watches, transfixed. When he finally returns to bed, the scene that burns behind his eyes is that of a Sisyphean struggle - people crawling on all fours, clawing their way up the mountain in a bid for survival. He dreams of apocalypse." My question from that is: Would that accurately describe life as you saw it in Srebrenica, taking the whole time you were there, a daily fight for survival?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a bit hard for me to go back to that period. You have to understand me. It's been several days now that I have been vividly living through this period of 1992 and 1993, which makes me exceptionally emotional, and it is sometimes hard for me to talk about these things. It's been going on for too long now in order for me to speak about these things with equanimity. This is the worst thing that ever happened to me in my life. I don't think anything worse than that can happen. It was literally from the month of December through to the period when the first convoys started coming in in late March 1993, it was virtually a struggle, an everyday struggle for survival. The people lost any emotions they had in them because they were overcome by their instincts. I am an eyewitness of the atrocities that took place in Srebrenica, something that people in general find very difficult to understand. This drive, this basic instinct of survival, is something terrible. I remember the first convoys that set out from Tuzla for Srebrenica, bringing food. It was late March 1993. As the convoy returned to Tuzla, it carried women, children, and elderly. It was a terrible sight. You could see mothers leaving their babies behind to clutch at the trucks and reach Tuzla, because Tuzla meant that they would be able to continue living. The children left behind were brought over to the hospital, and we were hardly in a position to take care of the children. I don't know what happened to them later on. But there were several cases where mothers left their own children behind just to ensure that they could go on living. It was the basest of instincts for survival. I've been telling you this in the past days as well, that this was a matter of study by psychologists, to see what takes place in people in an enclave, isolated, without the basic preconditions for normalcy. What happens to people when they become beasts, lose any sense of what it is to be humane. That is why I ask you to show consideration for me because it is very difficult for me to linger with my thoughts in that period. I would very much wish to forget the period, although I probably never will.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Well, I won't try to enter into too much vivid detail. In fact, the last subject which you're discussing I want to pick up. But firstly, just on the convoys to Tuzla, did you learn that people were actually crushed to death on the way to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser is rightly pointing to me that -- perhaps it's the case of, again, knowing what time period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, the witness was just referring to convoys which left in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it correct that that's in March 1993, that the convoys came in with food and left with people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones, because again, I'm -- Dr. Mujkanovic, are you all right? Are you all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it was late March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you are all right, whether we can continue, or whether you need a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue. We can continue. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please draw our attention straight away if you need a break. We fully understand that people who have lived through the trauma of war find it difficult to testify in a court of justice, particularly after the lapse of so many years. So any time you require a break, please let us know. Yes, Mr. Jones, I apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It was just that question, really: The convoys which left for Tuzla with people on board in March 1993, did you learn that people were actually crushed to death on the journey?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But you saw the convoys as they were leaving, as they were leaving Srebrenica. Would it be right to say that they were jam-packed with people?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They set out from Srebrenica, from outside the post office building. We had an agreement with Mr. Larry Hollingworth from UNPROFOR who coordinated these convoys, and the agreement was that one convoy should -- that is, one truck should be secured for the wounded. Usually a convoy had some ten trucks. So the first thing we wanted to ensure was to evacuate the wounded women and children, and for the rest of the trucks, the deal was that the refugees from Cerska and Konjevic Polje should have priority in leaving. They had already been there. Unfortunately, while arranging for this first convoy with Mr. Hollingworth, I thought that we would actually be able to achieve something, that we would have an orderly way of setting up the convoy, although it was made up of trucks. And I remember the trucks lined up in front of the post office building and the hospital, and then Mr. Larry Hollingworth and I climbed on top of the post office and we had a megaphone and we thought that we were going to coordinate the whole process and tell the people who should step forward and board the trucks. However, all of a sudden, the stampede started, where people started flocking to these trucks, trying to climb on top of them. And at a certain point, we couldn't control the whole process, and Mr. Hollingworth said everyone should leave, get off the trucks, or the convoy would not depart. Unfortunately, nobody wanted to leave, to dismount the trucks, so they simply had to have the convoy start. And as the convoy started, more people started flocking towards it and trying to clutch at the trucks. I escorted the truck with the wounded up until Potocari, and I remember that the drivers were trying to get organised as to who should start the truck first, and that's how they went ahead. That's how I knew what was going on with the convoy up until Potocari. But as the convoy proceeded, I wouldn't be able to tell you what happened to it. I can't tell you whether somebody got crushed or killed. I never heard any such thing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it right that Tony Birtley also filmed that scene?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He also filmed an interview with General Morillon, he filmed the attacks on Srebrenica, whatever was taking place at the time when he was filming. On the 1st or the 2nd of April, 1993, he was then severely wounded and operated on in the hospital in Srebrenica, together with the commander of the UNPROFOR forces who were there. I believe his name was Captain David McDonald, from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I believe you saved Tony Birtley's leg.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the stresses and strains of living through that period. As a medical practitioner, would you agree that the constant shelling, the food crisis, being under siege, affected the general mental health of the population, too?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've tried to explain this a couple of minutes ago. There was a total transformation of the mindset of the people. Their basic instinct surfaced, whereas their emotions disappeared. And of course, instincts -- it's the animals who are driven by their instincts, the instinct for survival particularly. And it was from this transformation of the people that all the other difficulties stemmed, all the rows and conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were asked on Monday about Kemal Mehmedovic, nicknamed Kemal from Pale. Was he also nicknamed Kemo?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you said he was a difficult personality with a very bad temper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, firstly, you told us of an instant where, from 30 metres away, he had what you thought might be a human head. On that subject, firstly, would you agree that, from what you saw from that distance, what Kemo could have been carrying could have been, I don't know, a Halloween mask or something resembling a head?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know the man. It was shortly after my arrival in Srebrenica. I didn't know who he was or who many of the other people were, in fact. I only got to know them later on. It was in the late afternoon hours, just before dusk. There was a truck carrying wounded. Many of them were wounded as a result of them stepping into a land-mine field, and many among them were amputees, so to say. For many of them, both legs had to be amputated. Since it was the period shortly after we had set up the hospital facility, we did not have a special area set aside for conducting a triage. I stepped outside for a minute to have a smoke, and then they told me that there was a truck full of wounded arriving. At that point, I repeat, there were many, many people in front of the hospital, because that's what always happened. Whenever wounded were brought in, people would flock to see if, among them, there were their relatives or friends. There was always as many as 200, 300 people in front of the hospital. And as the truck was trying to break through the crowd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. Please answer the question, because each time you're going to be here for two weeks. You've been complaining that you have been already too long here, but the way you're answering the questions, you're going to be here for two weeks. I hate to stop you, because I hate interrupting anyone, but we can't go on like this. It was a very simple question. When you saw Kemo holding something in his hand, which we have been given to understand was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or might have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- might have been a human head, do you have any doubt in your mind that it could have been something else and not a human head, but something resembling a human head, like a Halloween mask? Given the circumstances and what you saw, do you have any real doubt in your mind that it wasn't a human head? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot claim with certainty that it was a human head, but what struck me from the distance that I was looking at him was that it was a human head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he saying anything in regard to what he was holding in his hand? Kemo, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was far away from me, some 25 to 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't hear him say anything, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't hear what he was saying. I didn't know the man at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And you have no idea, do you, where he found that head, if it was a head; whether it was a Serb head, a Muslim head, or anything of that nature, do you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. I don't know if it was someone's head or not. I only told you what I saw and what made me believe that this is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, concerning Kemo, isn't it right that you became aware from the moment of your arrival in Srebrenica, or soon after, that there were a number of individuals like Kemo who were out of control?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Based on what you came to know of Kemo and his personality, do you agree that if Naser Oric, for example, had tried to control Kemo, he, Kemo, probably would have killed Oric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's speculation at its best, Mr. Jones. You either forget the question or you rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you were -- when you came to The Hague and spoke to the Office of the Prosecutor, didn't you express an opinion to them to the effect that if Naser Oric tried to control Kemo, Kemo probably would have killed him?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you confirm that opinion here?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One-hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned yesterday - I think it was yesterday or perhaps the day before - a Mrki, a Mrki Mandzic. Do you agree that there were quite a few people in Srebrenica with the nickname Mrki?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many Mrkis you knew or came across during your time in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three of whom I knew who were nicknamed Mrki.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you know Hazim Mrki from Voljevica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Hazim Mrki and Mrki Mandzic and Sabahudin Mrki, I knew them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turning to a different area altogether, I have a question about Serbs and their uniforms. We've already discussed uniforms on the Muslim side. Now, you told us that you treated wounded Serbs at the hospital. Isn't it correct that some of them were in civilian clothes but you ascertained that they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Which wounded are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wounded Serbs at the hospital who you treated.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Weren't some of them in civilian clothes but you formed the opinion, or you became aware, that they were, in fact, fighters or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never formed any opinion as to whether they were fighters or not. I simply regarded them as the wounded, brought into the hospital, rather than thinking about them being fighters or not. And I never talked to the wounded about what their capacity was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It was really just whether, in your experience, whether, on the Serb side, people were fighting who were not in uniforms. Is that something which you ever learned?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that there were also Serbs who were wounded, some of whom wore a uniform and others wore civilian clothes. Now, whether they were fighters or not, that's something I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. You went to forward command post, I believe, for certain actions, at least for Bjelovac, in December 1992; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Bjelovac. This area is not far from the hospital, up on a hill, perhaps some 5 to 6 kilometres away from the hospital. I wasn't at the forward command post of Bjelovac, or whatever it was called. I went over there with Ramiz Becirevic who wanted to look into the possible way of pulling out wounded and bringing them into the hospital. It wasn't an official forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I was wondering if, when you were in that position, in Zaluzje, were you able to observe the Serb military from there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. I was only able to see a line of people going in the direction of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. You told us that you saw Serb aeroplanes shooting on the people in Bjelovac; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Serb aircraft crossing the Drina and shooting, firing upon the people from machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you also see Serb aircraft dropping bombs on Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just saw one aircraft, so there was just this one aircraft that I saw, and they shelled and fired upon the people who were on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What kind of a plane was it? Can you describe the plane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not an expert in planes, but these were fighter planes. Now whether it was a MiG-21 or 29, but such planes bombed Srebrenica daily. I just don't know whether it was a 21 or a 29, I only know that they were very fast and that they were used to bomb the town itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're talking about -- I'm only limiting my question to the aircraft you saw dropping bombs on Bjelovac. Do you recall what kind of a plane it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the fighter planes, probably a MiG-21, perhaps 29, although I'm more inclined to think it was a 21, it's a fighter plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you exclude categorically that it could have been a biplane with a propeller, an engine propeller?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps we should fix the time as well when the witness made these observations, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you exclude this possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully exclude this possibility, Your Honour, because during everyday shelling, that is, bombing of Srebrenica, I was able to clearly distinguish between the different planes arriving to bomb Srebrenica. So this was definitely not a plane with a propeller.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please stick to Bjelovac, to the attack on Bjelovac. Stick to that one. I'm not asking you with regard to other instances when you saw planes. When you saw this plane in Bjelovac, so you exclude that it was a propeller aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do exclude the possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you be able to give us an indication at what time of the day it was that you saw aircraft bombing -- dropping bombs on Bjelovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Actually, I think it was fighter planes shooting. That's perhaps the confusion. He's referred to MiGs shooting on the population. I asked whether he had seen bombs dropped, and he said he hadn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said dropping bombs as well, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This occurred in the afternoon hours, early afternoon, it might have been perhaps 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it fighter planes shooting or also dropping bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't dropping bombs. There were missiles fired, and there was fire from a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we've heard enough on that. Yes, Mr. Jones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I may come back to it. In fact, I've skipped ahead in dealing with the actions to Bjelovac, and I actually want to go back and start with Jezestica and the time shortly after your arrival in Srebrenica. To do that, I want to look at another passage in War Hospital, and it's pages 83 to 84, and I'll just read the section: "Nedret, still wearing his green, blood-covered gown, strides out of the hospital to take a much-needed break. In all of his weeks on the front line near Tuzla, he has never experienced anything like this. There, he worked with trained surgical colleagues and had an advanced hospital close by. Here, the buck stops with him, but the commanders who chose to wage this all-out attack --" and that's clear from the context that's referring to Jezestica on the 8th of August, 1992 -- "don't seem to have considered this. He catches sight of one of them, Hakija Meholjic, climbing the hospital driveway to check on his injured soldiers. "'You should have warned me about the offensive!' Nedret yells at him. He would advised the commander to hold off until the medical team was prepared to receive casualties. 'You're waging war like Indians!' he says. He insists that soldiers include him in all future military planning." So I have several questions arising from that. First of all, do you recognise that as an account of an exchange which you had with Hakija Meholjic very shortly after your arrival in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this exchange. I really can't say whether the other person involved was Hakija Meholjic or not. The author of the book claims so. My impression, the way I remember it, it was actually Akif Ustic, the person I talked to. But this was a comment that I made. I knew nothing about anything, and then in the afternoon, suddenly, dozens of wounded began streaming in. I was quite unprepared. That's why I made the comment about them fighting like Indians. This is certainly something that I said at the time. I also said that we didn't need to know when actions would occur and be carried out, but that we should be told ahead of time so that we could prepare the hospital and ourselves to receive the wounded, the casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what any doctor would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's a reference there of you wanting to be involved in planning. Wasn't your concern simply to have adequate warning so you could prepare the hospital so as to be able to give people the best treatment?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I think what I asked for was perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It says there that "the commanders," plural, "who chose to wage this all-out attack..." Is it your understanding that the decision to attack Jezestica, if you know, was taken by a number of commanders?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is two days after my arrival. I knew none of those people, nor was I aware of the fact that there was an attack in the offing. I was just taken aback. I didn't know the people or that an attack was in the pipeline. I didn't know where this attack would occur. Suddenly, wounded people started coming in, and that's when I realised. But I can't tell you anything about them planning or not planning. The only comment I made at the time was the one you referred to, above.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to refer to an earlier passage in War Hospital, at page 80, again referring to this action, and I'll read it into the record: "Days after Nedret's arrival, the fighting around Srebrenica intensifies. Groups of local soldiers launch offensives and others fend off Chetnik advances. On August 8 --" that's 1992 -- "with the hospital already full, the staff overwhelmed, and part of the enclave under fire, a group of soldiers plans a surprise raid on the Serb village of Jezestica, where Serb soldiers have directed cannon fire at a neighbouring Muslim village for months. The action begins around noon. Some Srebrenicans stumble into a minefield and are carried back to the hospital. The remaining soldiers, many of them friends or family members of the dozens of Muslim men executed by Serbs in nearby Glogova at the start of the war, fire off a grenade and rush the village. Hand-to-hand fighting ensues, and casualties mount." Now, my questions following from that are based on the fact that you were in the hospital, weren't you, when this action happened, and you were receiving the wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I learn the question? Because there is a question mark but I'm not -- I don't know the question as such, or do I mistake it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is being asked -- I'm sorry. I take it that he is being asked, with reference to the paragraph or the section that has been read out to him, to the events mentioned therein, whether he was, when this action happened, whether he was in hospital and whether he was receiving the wounded from that particular military operation or action, whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I can understand it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, would you like me to repeat the question to you, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be fine, Your Honour. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The question is this: You've heard Mr. Jones read out to you from page 80 of this book about military activity in Jezestica at a particular time, and you were being asked, since this paragraph mentions wounded persons, persons getting wounded, you were being asked whether you were in hospital at the time this event occurred, and whether you were receiving the wounded for treatment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, did you hear from the wounded that they had attacked Jezestica because there was artillery there which had been directing cannon fire at neighbouring Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't in touch at the time, and the people who were coming in were seriously wounded. There must be records of what we did at the hospital on that day. There were three parallel tables on which we performed leg amputations. These people had strayed into a minefield, and dozens of people came in whose legs had been blown to bits. It was a scene of chaos at the hospital. I didn't even know who they had been attacked by or why the attack had taken place. It was as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just on that subject, very briefly, isn't it right that you had to perform amputations without anaesthetics because you didn't have that equipment?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only a matter of amputations. All sorts of surgery, over 600 operations, were performed with no anaesthetics to hand, opening up people's heads, people's stomachs, amputating their limbs. Later on, when we got some anaesthetics, those were no first-rate anaesthetics but a diluted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that you had to amputate because of the risk of gangrene setting in very quickly?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have bled to death had we not performed surgery, no question about that, especially those who had been wounded in the stomach. If you don't open their stomach immediately, they would soon die. It was a matter of days, maybe two, three, or four days, but they would have been dead. That much is certain. And this way at least they survived, even if they had to be operated on with no anaesthetics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that you also didn't have material for blood transfusions?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that that also caused a much higher level of fatalities than would otherwise be the case?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That much is certain. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just sticking with this action and the wounded which you received a bit longer, and only if you can help, do you recall receiving any wounded who were from Jaglici, Cizmici, or Glogova, any of those villages?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the specific villages. When I think back, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remember one wounded particularly, Dalibor Djozic, nicknamed Zele. An anti-aircraft gun shot him in the left upper arm. During night hours, he was brought in and I had to amputate his upper arm. This lad formed an emotional tie with me after that, so he stayed at the hospital and his left upper arm had to be amputated. I remember that person very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he from Jaglici, Cizmici, or Glogova?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was from a place called Kazan, which is a neighbourhood in Srebrenica not far from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That doesn't help you at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's jump to something else, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that Zele a civilian policeman later on, later on in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not sure that someone who did not have an arm could work as a police officer. I don't think he actually had a job. He just moved about town. He had been a drummer before the war, so he was quite a popular person. But I guess this made it impossible for him to keep on playing music. I don't think I've ever seen a police officer without an arm. But if you say so, it should be possible to prove and verify what he actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I have one final question concerning this incident, and I'm going to look at page 82 of War Hospital. Again, this is dealing with the wounded from the action on Jezestica. It reads: "Some patients stopped breathing as if paralysed while their hearts continue beating and blue blood oozes from their wounds. The doctors suspect that the Serbs used chemical weapons in the counterattack. The Yugoslav Army is known to have weaponised several chemical agents, including the nerve agent sarin. Doctors try injecting some of the patients with atropine, a medicine that blocks nerve receptors overstimulated by the chemical agent. It helps some of the men, but not the one Fatima --" and that's Dalbasic -- "is trying to save, who dies." Now, given that you were in the ward that day, treating patients, were you one of the doctors who treated these people and who suspected that the Serbs were using Sarin, a deadly nerve gas in the counterattack on Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one thing that we couldn't find an explanation for at the time. During the amputations, first the blood would change colour; then there would be patients who simply stopped breathing and died right there on the table. We tried to find an explanation for these sudden changes in their behaviour as patients who had been wounded, the reactions of their body during the actual operation. We thought that maybe poisons had been used, and that's why we tried to counter the effect of these poisons, to re-establish the normal breathing functions during an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And subsequent to that, during the rest of your time in Srebrenica, did you ever become aware that the Serbs were using chemical weapons against the enclave?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not something that I can state categorically. This would require a very thorough medical study and a well-founded expert opinion. My speculation would lead to nothing. There were strange forms of behaviour by patients, strange things that would happen during their treatment or the operation itself, something that might have indicated things like the use of nerve gas or poison. But this is not something that I could state or ascertain offhand, like this, with no thorough examination of the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, just on that subject, in July 1995, were you in Tuzla when the column of people arrived from Srebrenica, after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you become aware of stories from the people who fled Srebrenica that chemical weapons had been used against them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what's the relevance of all this, what happened in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The indictment goes right until the end of 1995, and a large number of my questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's your client who is being accused --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Of course, Your Honour. Our client is charged under Article 7.3 of the Statute on the basis of command responsibility, and relevant to those charges is the whole command environment, what the strength and deployment of the enemy forces were, what he could do under those circumstances. And so the fact that there is a foe which is deploying chemical weapons against the population is pertinent to the general situation. If that's a problem, I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, if you look at Counts 1 and 2, they are very specific as regards a time frame. If you look at Counts 3 to 6, they are also very specific as regards to events and time frame. So I don't see how this -- what might have happened - I'm not saying that it didn't - but what might have happened in 1995 could have a bearing on --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a matter which I'd prefer not to discuss in front of the witness. We can raise it at another stage. The date 1995 certainly appears in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it will, but the indictment is what it is and the counts are what they are, and they are very specific, particular to events and to dates. So I would suggest that you move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll move on to the Podravanje action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as the Podravanje action was concerned, didn't hay, bricks, and other essential items get destroyed by the torbari [Realtime transcript read in error "tobari"], if I can refer to them that way, despite requests by the army, or by the fighters, that those items be gathered?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- yesterday, we already referred to that issue through questioning by the Prosecution. Now, when it comes to the Podravanje action, we have the testimony of a witness that there is an action and there is a time before and a time after. When he gave testimony yesterday, he was specific in his testimony when it comes to the time, so it should be also very specific in the question, I would suggest and advise. And whenever there is within the question also a confirmation needed for a qualification, like torbari, that that should be another question. So no question within questions, and with the vagueness of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take them one by one, and I'm sure that Mr. Jones will agree with me. Let's take torbari, and not "tobari" as it appears in the transcript; torbari. I would suggest that you first ask the witness whether he has ever heard the word "torbari," and if he has, what does he mean by "torbari," so that we at least are sure, and the Prosecution too, that we are on the same wave length. We'll start with that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then if afterwards I could be given a few moments to read Mr. Wubben's objection so I can understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can give you an adjournment, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I'll need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start. Have you ever heard of the word "torbari"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you understand by the word "torbari"? I'm sorry, I'm taking over for this simple part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm happy for you to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does "torbari" mean? What is your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a generic name for those people over there. They carried bags slung over their shoulders or on their backs. They would enter villages prior to or after an operation, looting food and taking food and foodstuffs away. That's what they did. And these are the civilians that I was talking about yesterday who would wait for the army to seize control of a village before storming the village themselves. Then they would pick stuff up and they would leave. Carpetbaggers, the so-called carpetbaggers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I were to look into a dictionary of your language, would I find the word "torbari"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you would, but I don't believe you would find the same meaning described. "Torbar," a very simple explanation would be, a person carrying a bag. That's all there is to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, this word "torbari," did it already exist before the war or was it invented in that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the first time I heard the word used. I had never heard the word used before, not in the same meaning, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the rest of the objection made by Mr. Wubben, I, too, feel a little bit confused, Mr. Wubben, what you mean. Could you explain? Because it looked to me more of a suggestion to Mr. Jones than an objection. I can't understand what you meant, to be honest. Perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, the question by Mr. Jones referred to the destruction in a view -- in particular with a view to an action. Now, yesterday we learned from the witness testifying in court that he was -- he witnessed certain events happening not directly through the combat action, or when the combat action took place, but after that. Now, when the question refers to a specific action, and a question relates to -- includes the fact that hay had been destroyed during that action, or suggests that, then the answering should be very specific and pointed out that yesterday he testified that he was only present after the action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, I know what you mean now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm still not sure if I -- an objection which takes 10 lines to state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is an objection, it is an objection. In actual fact, the objection is that you shouldn't be asking the witness questions relating to events that he was not present at when they happened. And Mr. Wubben is saying that yesterday, or whenever it was, the witness, with regard to this military action, arrived on the spot only at a certain point in time, when certain things had already happened and others started happening or were happening in front of his eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. But that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he's asking you to split the question and not to mix together in one basket what he couldn't have seen because he wasn't there and what he could have seen because he saw -- he told us he saw it yesterday. This is more or less how I am understanding. I am not suggesting at any time - don't misunderstand me, Mr. Wubben - that you were not clear in your objection, but I'm not suggesting that you are deficient either, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's why I'm somewhat puzzled, because do I understand Mr. Wubben to be arguing that there's a hearsay rule, and witnesses are not able to speak about things that they didn't see themselves? Because surely this witness can speak about things he learned before, after -- the Prosecution showed this witness many documents months before he arrived, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- let's go to the question that you had, and if necessary, I'll take it up myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I have questions framed already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, you told us that Zulfo Tursunovic wanted hay to be preserved before the Podravanje action so that refugees would have hay to feed their horses with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only their horses; livestock in general, including cows.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And despite that, you saw the torbari - and I'll use that term - destroying hay and other material which could have been used to feed livestock; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw people do that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it also true that you saw dead bodies of Serbs in Podravanje, and that all of the ones you saw were in uniform, except for the body of one woman?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it also true that, as far as you're aware, looting and destruction by the torbari was still occurring days after the military action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't the fighters from Srebrenica also capture a tank from the Serbs in Podravanje?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you're aware, was that tank captured from the Bracan elevation, above the bauxite mine?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where it was captured. I know that it was captured, and I saw it right there, while I was still in the Podravanje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And isn't it right --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tank had an anti-aircraft gun, a three-barrelled gun, attached to it, 20/3. There was a tank, and behind the tank there was an anti-aircraft gun attached to it. The type was 20/3, that was the type of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I see the time, Your Honour, and it might be an appropriate moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. We'll reconvene --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There will be a 30-minute break during which time the three Judges will be having a meeting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Apologies for the delay, but we were still in camera discussing one -- two of the pending motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I'll try to ask you very brief questions and you can provide brief answers, and hopefully we'll make enough progress here that we can be finished with your testimony on Monday. Now, referring to this tank which was captured in Podravanje, isn't it right that the driver of the tank was -- sorry, let me rephrase that, that a Muslim fighter tried to drive the tank and he was somewhat inexperienced and he drove over a woman's body, smashing her head.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: After the action in Podravanje, didn't the Serbs retaliate with massive shelling, as well as aerial bombardment, of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned on Tuesday how people from Suceska were involved in the Podravanje action. Isn't it right that Suceska is right by Podravanje?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you aware, or did you become aware, that the Muslims in Suceska were getting shelled by the Serbs in Podravanje in the days and weeks before the action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you said that Zulfo's unit was probably in Podravanje because you received a lot of wounded who were from Suceska. Is it right that not all able-bodied men from Suceska were necessarily in Zulfo's unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you also receive a lot of wounded who were from villages in the Vlasenica municipality; for example, Dzile, Stedra, Nurici?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider all these to be Suceska, because Suceska comes under the municipality of Vlasenica. Now, I cannot speak of the individual and specific villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's talk about the action in Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992, and if I can preface my question by going back to something you said earlier. You said that the worst situation of starvation was in early 1993, but is it right that even in October 1992, there was a severe food crisis in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, throughout the period, in fact. But it did peak in December, January, February, March, therefore, end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993. But throughout the period there was shortage of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So did you understand that the Fakovici action specifically was carried out because of the vital need for resources - food, ammunition, weapons?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only this action. I said that practically all the actions were carried out because there was need for food, ammunition, and other things. So I would not pick out just the Fakovici action, but I would rather highlight that all the actions were carried out in order to obtain food, ammunition, and medicines, so that this was always the goal before and after the Fakovici action. I also said that this area was under nobody's control, not even the military, and the civilians were basically present in the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. And so when I come to the Bjelovac and Kravica actions, I won't revisit this theme. I take it from your answer that they were also actions carried out for food and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in Fakovici, you learned, didn't you, that two or three four-barrelled anti-aircraft guns and many weapons were captured from the Serbs in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that I learnt of the Fakovici action only when the wounded started arriving. Zulfo Tursunovic was one of them, and he told me that he had captured one four-barrelled gun. I don't know how many, in fact, were captured. But he told me how it had happened that he was wounded; that he was basically on his way to capture the four-barrelled gun, and in the process he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you understand that a lot of food and a lot of medicines were also captured at Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain amount of medicines and medical supplies were brought in, in fact, but I cannot speak of the quantities of food that were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move on to the Bjelovac action. Still, one more question on Fakovici. This phenomenon you've described, sociological phenomenon, of the torbari following the fighters into towns after actions, is that also the same phenomenon, as far as you know, which took place in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This phenomenon was a recurring one. And not only did they enter into villages after the fighters, sometimes they would go to these villages before actions. And that's why sometimes we would basically have civilians brought in as wounded before the fighters that were wounded came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turning to Bjelovac and the action on the 14th of -- 14th to 19th December, 1992, is it a fair summary of what you've told us that this action concentrated on Muslim villages that had been occupied by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you learn from Muslims from that area who had fled to Srebrenica that, in early 1992, the Serbs had ethnically cleansed thousands of them from that area?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear -- I did learn.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you hear that when the Serbs expelled the Muslims, they often stole the Muslims' livestock and belongings as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were Srebrenica, because the Serbs first entered Srebrenica which was then liberated. I knew that they had set on fire the entire neighbourhoods of the town. Now, as for the Muslim villages and whether they had been looted or not, I really can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear that the Serbs had a massive military presence in this area, along the Drina? And I'm talking about the period in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The so-called Drina Corps was concentrated over there, and of course a corps is a large military formation that can number several tens of thousands of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There were, weren't there, a lot of corn fields in this area?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very fertile area, on the left bank of the Drina River. It is a plain where the population mostly farmed the land, cultivating grain, vegetables, fruit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you hear or understand, learn, that the corn had not been harvested by the Muslims because they had been forced out in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did learn about this, and there were many people from those parts who would, at night, prior to the actions that had taken place there, go into the fields, harvest the corn, and then return to Srebrenica. Because I've already told you that there would be a night or two nights that would be calm, and then the third night, mines would be laid along the corridors where it was known that the civilians would usually pass. And then, as a result of that, you would have a great many civilians mutilated, and many of them actually got killed in the minefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did the Serbs also put booby-traps in the fields and also in the cellars, which would be triggered when Muslims tried to go back and get food?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it happened. First they would let them pass across the certain area, and then -- thus luring them, and in the end, would lure them into such traps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, just dealing with what you know, did that create a pressure, pressure from these civilians, on the fighters to go in and secure the area so that they could safely gather food?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer this question. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. Now, did you also learn that Bjelovac was successful because of the surprise tactic of fighters going around from the Drina and taking the Serbs by surprise?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was, roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I understand, and correct me if I'm wrong, that you did have conversations with some of the fighters who participated in the action, and they told you a lot of what had happened. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I spoke to Safet Omerovic, who was one of the participants in this battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And his nickname is Mis; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he tell you that a frontal attack from the hills was not being contemplated because the Serbs had fortified their positions in the village?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained this in my earlier testimony here. The civilians, as soon as they realised that there was chaos in this particular area, they managed to break through the lines. And I said that it was a multitude of people going in the direction of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't Mis tell you that they had eliminated a barracks of soldiers which also had armoured vehicles, and that they captured a tank and two APCs in Bjelovac? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He told me about it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you'll bear with me for a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've spoken a bit about planes which you saw, fighter planes. We've already had detail about that, so I'm not going to go into any great detail, but isn't it right that what you saw were fighter planes from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did see the direction they came from, or rather, I'm speaking about this one plane that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how long were you --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, if this is the specific event we're talking about. Now, in the course of Srebrenica being bombed, I saw several types of planes, because Srebrenica was exposed to at least 50 air raids. The planes involved included the ones mentioned by His Honour, but there were other smaller planes also involved in the attacks on Srebrenica, because they would usually fly in pairs.
