They'd be active from a higher altitude so that anti-aircraft guns could not reach them. They were out of their range, because their range was some 2.000 metres, and above that the ammunition would simply disperse. So it will be from that altitude that they would bomb Srebrenica. And now, when you would have fighter planes, those were MiGs flying very fast, and as they would bomb Srebrenica, they would basically raze to the ground the entire building. It's true that there were two types of planes; there were those with propellers and then the other ones that I suppose were MiGs, because that's what the JNA had, it had fighter planes, MiG 21 and 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm asking you now about Bjelovac. If you could just remind us when you made these observations, and for how long? Of airplanes. You said in the afternoon, and then for how long? How long were you watching?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very brief. We were able to follow the attack which lasted less than a minute, because the plane fired, made its attack, and then looped, turned around, and went in the direction of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it caused a great number of casualties among the Muslim civilians; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you referred to this biplane, the plane referred to by His Honour, and you appeared to be aware of that biplane or biplanes. Were you ever aware of where the biplanes were flying from, were taking off from?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent we heard or knew, based on intelligence that was known around Srebrenica, they'd take off from a locality near Bratunac, called Stale. That was the -- perhaps not the official name of the area, but that's how it was known. Now, the fighter planes, MiGs, took off from the Ponikve airport in Serbia, airfield in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware that the fighting in Bjelovac lasted about four days?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lasted long, at least three to four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you gather, from speaking to fighters who fought in Bjelovac, that there was fierce resistance from the Serbs and a counterattack from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the details concerning the fighting, but I know that actions usually lasted one or two days. But this particular one lasted longer. I remember that we were under great pressure in the hospital. Now, I didn't go into details to analyse whether this was due to a counterattack. I know that it lasted three or four days. There were many wounded, among whom many were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, wasn't Hakija Meholjic in Sase for this action, firstly?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His unit was tasked with going to Sase, and later on I went to Sase with Hakija, when they were pulling out some goods from a storage facility there. This was after the -- in the new year. They were taking some generators for power, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Did you gather from Hakija, or from men in his unit, that they captured a huge amount of items, such as food, weapons, howitzers, and multiple rocket-launchers? I'm afraid you have to give a verbal answer.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this when they brought it over in front of the Domavija Hotel. I told you that I stayed at the Domavija Hotel and would return there every night. I believe that in addition to foodstuffs, they captured large amounts of detergents, soap, and other such items. And I saw that there was a four-barrelled gun, a 20/4 type of a gun in front of the hotel. I also saw a modified multiple rocket-launcher practically made from a missile launcher dismounted from a plane. So it wasn't a classical JNA multiple rocket-launcher, it was a remodeled, refashioned one that they had captured. I believe it was of 60 millimetre in calibre. That's what the missiles were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was a howitzer also captured?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see a howitzer there, so I can't tell you whether they had captured it or not. I told you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you also aware that a tank and two APCs were captured in Sase?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was aware of this, and I did see them driving the two APCs as they came into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you understand Sase to be a major Serb stronghold?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say whether Sase was a major Serb stronghold.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to move on to Kravica, and just a few questions about Kravica, although I may come back to it on Monday. And if we could look at pages 108 to 109 of War Hospital, I'm just going to read one short passage there, starting at the bottom of page 108. And it's stated -- I'll wait until you have it. The bottom, the bottom paragraph: "With aid convoys on hold and Serb forces engaging in a strong counterattack, supplies peter out. The doctors horde the remaining medicines. Almost a month after the last convoy, food is again in desperately short supply. Srebrenica soldiers plan an offensive on Serb villages, calculating the expected weight and types of goods that might be captured in different places. They choose January 7, Serb Orthodox Christmas, the second time they have launched an attack on an Orthodox holiday. And they choose Kravica, a historic centre for Serb nationalism whose inhabitants fought against the Ottoman Empire in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and armed and trained local Serbs for this war." Did you understand from fighters you spoke to that that date, Orthodox Christmas, was selected, again, for the element of surprise?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you understand the action in Kravica to be driven by the desperate need for food?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said before, that all the actions had, as their objective, the search for food.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you also understand Kravica to be a historic centre for Serb nationalism and the place where local fighters had been armed and trained for this war, the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that Kravica was a centre of Serb nationalism, but I knew that before the war, some seven to eight months before the outbreak of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1991, Kravica could not be passed through, that it had been blocked, that two Bosniaks had been killed there as they were on their way from Konjevic Polje to Kravica, so that even before the official outbreak of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was an incident in Kravica. And although this took place on the main road, the police were unable to do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't it right that you were told about what happened in Kravica -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just apologise and say this: If I were to say that Kravica was a centre of Serb nationalism in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I might, by doing so, offend those at Pale, because they would consider Pale to be a centre, or those in Srebrenica. So I can say that Kravica was one of the places where Serb nationalism was prominent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did Zele, you mentioned earlier, did he tell you about the Kravica action?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Zele might have been one of those who told me various things about the action, but Zele was an amputee. One of his arms was amputated. It was Mis who told me about the Kravica action. It was after the action that he came to see me at the hospital and told me all about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he tell you that a haystack was lit on fire as a signal?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This was a signal for the start of the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that sometimes -- or let's deal with Kravica, that this was also to send a signal to the Serbs to leave the area? When they would see something burning, they would understand that there was an attack and they would then flee?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to claim either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But are you aware that a way was left out for the Kravica Serbs, namely, towards the Drina, towards the north, so that they could flee without being entirely encircled?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of these details either. I wouldn't be able to state either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And then finally, on Kravica, I think you've told us this already, but wasn't it only after Kravica fell that Srebrenica was linked up with Cerska and Kamenica and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A safe corridor was established between Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica, and further on up towards Cerska, but not a corridor that could be used for traffic along the road. It was a corridor which actually ran across the hill, and then from Konjevic Polje on to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that hill, is that Ravni Buljim, or is that another path?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had to take the road that I took across Gornji Potocari or Buljim. It's just one road, but there are several ways to take that road. You can go a bit further to the left or to the right. It was just a corridor. You had to pass Kravica in order to get to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, after Kravica fell, isn't it right that the Serbs launched a massive counterattack?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you aware of a winter offensive which was launched by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I'd like to show a document to the witness. It's D184. It's a document of the War Presidency, dated 17th January, 1993, and the ERN is 01858496.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this is titled "Protest." Just looking at the content of the document, would you first agree that this is the sort of appeal for help being sent out from Srebrenica which you referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say, I've never seen this document before. If I may just be allowed two or three minutes to go through it and see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this document refers to a number of things, but, among others, massive artillery and air attacks on Srebrenica from the Serbs, including by forces from Uzice, with tanks, et cetera. Was that the situation in Srebrenica at the time, in the Srebrenica enclave at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I said that in my statement also. Srebrenica was subjected to daily shellings by mortar and long-range artillery pieces positioned in Serbia. Air strikes too for a while were a daily reality. Five past three, you could set your alarm clock, because that was when the air strikes would regularly start. So yes, it is quite true to say that Srebrenica was both bombed and shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You agreed that after the 7th of January, Srebrenica was linked up with Konjevic Polje, Kamenica, and Cerska. Isn't it right that in this period, those enclaves, that Konjevic Polje, Kamenica, and Cerska were greatly under threat in this period, middle of January 1993 and onwards?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the whole area of the Cerska and Konjevic Polje enclaves shared Srebrenica's fate. They were spared no attacks and no shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wasn't Naser Oric in fact away from Srebrenica for a lot of this period, from January the 17th, 1993, through February and March, precisely because he was on the front lines, fighting to stop the Serb advance?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this protest, it refers to an offensive which was carried out in the south-east of the Srebrenica enclave, whereas Konjevic Polje and Cerska are in the north. Therefore, it's very difficult to see these things tally, I mean what happened in Konjevic Polje on the one hand and what happened in the south-east of the enclave, in Skelani. It's true that the offensive was first launched in Skelani, but I have no idea what was happening in Konjevic Polje and Cerska at the time. It's really difficult for me to say whether an attack was under way there, too. I'm not perfectly clear about all these things, but here I am, and we can seek to clarify this together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I can concentrate more specifically on Naser Oric and the extent to which you saw him in January, February, March 1993. So my question was, really: Isn't it true that with these offensives going on, he was not in the town of Srebrenica very much during that period?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the previous days, I said that I would see Naser whenever he came to the hospital. That was how we usually met. He always came to the hospital after an action or a battle, no matter whether offensive or defensive. He would visit the fighters. We would have a conversation, that sort of thing. As for the period of time that you have suggested, it's very difficult for me to say. I'd be speculating to tell you that I saw more or less of him during that particular period. I did see him occasionally. Whenever he returned after these battles, that was when and where we met. Sometimes we met in town, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned, in the context of recognising Naser Oric's signature, that at a certain time, you were receiving messages from him precisely because he wasn't able to come to the hospital, and my question is: Weren't there more of these messages in that period --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- weren't there more of these messages in this early 1993 period than in 1992, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The messages were sporadic. They were at their most frequent during the evacuation of the wounded from Srebrenica, which was supposed to take place in March. This failed on account of Serb shelling, several times. That was when I received most of these messages. But again, I can't specify how frequent they were in a certain period, or when they were less frequent. But this was not our usual means of communication. It was only when he couldn't personally make it to the hospital to discuss things with me that he would send a message. Therefore, it's very difficult for me to see the messages in relation to any particular event, except for the evacuation at the time when the fiercest fighting was going on in the south-east of the enclave. This was an example of a time period when he was not able to come to the hospital personally, and those were usually the times that I received messages from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And, sorry, in what period was that, roughly?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the messages, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The period when you say the fiercest fighting was going on in the south-east of the enclave, can you give us a time period for that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From mid-February to on or about the 17th of April, that was the fiercest offensive that was ever carried out against Srebrenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right, then, that between mid-February and mid-April 1993, you saw less of Naser Oric than you had done previously?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Because he wasn't visiting the hospital, I take it.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, moving to a different area now, and in fact slightly back in time, we have a video. It's Prosecution Exhibit V000-3939. It's just three minutes long. It's P318.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I should ask the booth, I think, to switch to Defence mode. If the technical booth could give me an indication when it's on everyone's screens, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For once I had hoped there are no technical problems, but there are. So we will all need to wait a couple of minutes, I think, until this is all sorted out. The technician is on his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A couple of minutes doesn't pose a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, I mean there is nothing we can do from here, from our end, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I think the technical hitch wasn't so major. Perhaps you could freeze -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to play the video, but I'll just freeze it there just for identification purposes. Do you recognise the figure in the middle?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's Naser Oric, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I believe, when we play the video, we'll see that you were present at this gathering. Do you recognise the other people on Naser Oric's left as being a Dutch journalist and his driver?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph that I'm looking at, you mean the one on the right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bearded man.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Naser Oric's left, yes, that is, indeed, a journalist who came to Srebrenica in the early days. I think it was in August. It was just after I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So could the date on the screen be correct, 19 August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can see the date. I'm sure that it was in August. I'm just not sure whether it's the 18th or the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll play the video for three minutes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies, we're not going to play the full three minutes, we're going to stop it before then. Stop it there, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This is simply a question about physical appearances. Would you agree, firstly, that Naser Oric had at that time, August 1992, a rather distinctive fringe - I don't want to say anything insulting to my client - but a rather stringy fringe, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a little beard too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did he have that beard the whole time that you knew him in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll play a bit further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is perhaps not the best frame to choose.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I just have a question, in looking at this video, do you agree that that man looks a lot like Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But it's not him, is it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not him. There were a lot of people who looked a little like Naser, bearded people, that sort of styling. Crew-cut, short hair, beards, it was a fashion back then, you could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't that right, that there were, in fact, if I may put it this way, Naser-imitators, people who adopted his look?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, very much so. He was their idol. They styled themselves after him in terms of haircut, in terms of their beards, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's all we're showing of the video. While we're on Naser's physical appearance, would you agree that he's about 180 centimetres tall?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must be 184, and he's just slightly shorter than I am, which would make it about 180, yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And while we're at it, would you agree that he has brown eyes?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been long since I last saw his eyes, but I think they're probably brown, a dark brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we saw Naser Oric there in the video. He wasn't surrounded by armed bodyguards or anything of that nature; is that right? From when you saw him in the town, he didn't go around with tens of armed bodyguards?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. I'm not aware whether or not we saw from the video that he was not surrounded by armed bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the objection needs to be sustained. The video only shows one particular spot, we don't know about the rest, so it's easy to rephrase your question, Mr. Jones, and ask him whether it was the norm for Mr. -- for your client to be surrounded by bodyguards or not, and whether he was surrounded by bodyguards on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'll take Your Honour's first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it normal for Naser Oric to be surrounded by bodyguards?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who they were. I'm not familiar with any people that may have been Naser Oric's bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'm actually going to move to another area now. I'm going to look at some documents. We have plenty of time. You were shown a lot of documents, and you told us in a number of cases that the signature was similar to that or resembled that of Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, with Your Honours' permission, I'd be grateful if we could conduct an exercise which is, if the cameras could just show our legal assistant here for a moment, we're just going to conduct an exercise, the purpose of which will be obvious in due course. I don't know if the camera is able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's just wait and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I think I know what's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If you know, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I would rather wait, I would rather wait, before I will let you say what the objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, could the usher please take a piece of paper and show it to the witness. If it could be placed on the ELMO. I can explain, Your Honour. I can anticipate the Prosecution's objection, and I'll explain very clearly the purposes of this exercise. This witness has been asked whether certain signatures resembled that of Naser Oric, or were similar to. We have a signature which we would like to ask the witness whether it's similar to or resembles that of Naser Oric. I don't see how there can be any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So the question is, Dr. Mujkanovic, do you agree that that signature resembles or is similar to that of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one looks very much like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'd ask for that to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All of them or ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which ones of them? All of them or some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I may show exactly which one. This one sort of doesn't, but this one really does. [Indicates]. And then this one and this one, and all the rest. The top two perhaps Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't quite look like it, but the remaining four very much resemble his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. If that could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just a short -- to clarify. There was no objection from my side, it was a request for clarification for the exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at the end of the day, I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's the way -- how he put it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because at the end of the day, the more professional the forgery, the more resemblance there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the point is an obvious one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, turning to one of the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, first we'll need an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So D201.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, with the usher's assistance, could the witness be shown P176, please. That's ERN 03720933.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you said on Monday that the operational staff was, you thought, established in late September 1992. Now, this document is dated the 3rd of September, 1992. So isn't it right that this document, that the date on this document as the date of the establishment of the operations staff doesn't seem right to you, it seems too early?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems too early, yes. As far as I know, this occurred in mid-September 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I hate to have to intervene, but although the document bears a date as -- the date of the 3rd of September, 1992, if you read point 3, it says "The Chief of Staff is authorised to establish and start the work of the operations staff of the Srebrenica armed forces, by the 17th of September, at the latest." So we are basically talking of mid-September, as the witness says.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm coming to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 4 of that document, it says: "The operations staff, headed by Osman Osmanovic, might be united into an integral entity." Firstly, are we right to understand that as meaning integral within the Srebrenica staff? It's envisaged that the operations staff would be integrated into the Srebrenica staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I do not know what my learned friend means with "Srebrenica staff," while his is "armed forces staff" at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben is right, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would that be correct, that it was envisaged that the operations staff might be united into an integral entity with the Srebrenica armed forces staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of. The operations staff was set up and worked as an operations staff. I'm not sure what it was supposed to become part of or not. I'm not sure exactly what they mean by uniting the staff into an integral entity. I'm not sure what they mean by the establishing of a command body and this necessity that they seem to be discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Is it right that the operational staff was established as a parallel to the OS staff, the armed forces staff, as opposed to being established by the armed forces staff, so that there were two staffs?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer this question. I don't know, and I don't think I'm clear about this. Osman Osmanovic was the chief of the operations staff, and we know the members. If there was a parallel staff that was functioning at the same time, it's really not something that I can comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we might come back to that when we look at the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the moment, could the witness please be shown P8, which is 01239518.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in this document, it appears the president of the War Presidency is appointing Osman Osmanovic to the chief of staff of the Srebrenica armed forces. Firstly, Naser Oric isn't appointing Osman Osmanovic, is he, in this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, on Monday, you told us that "The supreme commander of the armed forces is the War Presidency." So is that right, that the supreme authority in Srebrenica was the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Are we talking now about the military, the civil authority or another authority? Please, Defence counsel should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I understand Mr. Jones' question, he's limiting himself to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. My question, and in fact it's a question which the witness can probably help us with, but that this was the supreme body above all civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, all right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The highest organ of authority is the civilian authority and the War Presidency. That was the highest body of authority in Srebrenica. Therefore, the military authorities were subordinated to the civilian authorities. That's how I believe -- that's what I believe the case was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, that's clear. Now, this document is dated the 14th of October, 1992, and it says, at paragraph 4, that "the tenure of Osman Osmanovic is to commence on the 14th of October, 1992," and at 5, it says that the decision comes into effect on the day of its adoption. So, in other words, and is this your understanding, that Osman Osmanovic was, in fact, appointed to his post on the 14th of October?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what one can conclude on the basis of this document. That was the de jure situation, but de facto, Osman Osmanovic assumed his duties in late September 1992, which means before the War Presidency actually issued its decision appointing him, that is to say, one month earlier. But I can perhaps clarify this. The War Presidency met approximately once a month, and probably this item appeared on their agenda scheduled for the 14th of October. This might be one of the explanations why this actually took place one month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If we can perhaps look at the war diary, at least a couple of pages of what's been described as the war diary. It's P84. For the record, the ERN for the entire war diary is 02115040 - 02115173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which particular page would you like to refer to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. 02115050, so about ten pages into the document. And I should just say that we requested a re-translation of certain parts of the war diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can perhaps deal with that on another occasion, because it doesn't concern any of the passages that I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I asked whether this matter needed to be discussed here, and I got the impression that it might later on but not necessarily at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps as a preliminary on Monday or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's all right. It's all right. I understand its importance, Mr. Jones, and we will discuss it in due course. I didn't raise it myself, although I discussed it with my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's page 5040. This is a meeting on the 14th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the best thing is to have the corresponding page in English. Do you know the corresponding page in English, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid not. The copy I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If I may help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: If it is 5040, then it is page 0309070 and 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't get that. What does that mean, 030907 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And then 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We have page 42 at the end for the B/C/S version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So from there it's -- might be where to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Due to the fact that I normally work from the electronic copy, I just used the B/C/S ERN, and it also means that I don't have my copy in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But I have a note that we see on that page, 5050, "The meeting was called to order by O. Osmanovic. He said we were faced with problems regarding the functioning of the system, War Presidency, two staffs, civilian protection." I don't know if you see that, Dr. Mujkanovic. "The meeting was called to order by O. Osmanovic. He said we were faced with problems regarding the functioning of the system, War Presidency, two staffs, civilian protection."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: This relates to the question I posed earlier, whether that reference to two staffs would be to the operations staff and staff of the Srebrenica armed forces, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Objections, Your Honour. This question includes something the witness already clarified, that he isn't aware of any other staff beside the operations staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It might jog his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Jones. The objection that has been raised by Mr. Wubben has a lot of sense too, eh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: You were a member of the operations staff, weren't you, Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the operations staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems to be what Mr. Wubben told us, 03090706, but I can't find the words or the part that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's certainly there in the Bosnian, because the witness has found it. As I say, I'm working from a different version. If it poses a problem, Your Honour, we can come back to this on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I find the quotation mentioned by my learned friend, it's under translation 03090711. There we have the minutes of the meeting in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And there is the agenda, paragraph 1, and the next sentence is, I believe, quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Wubben. That is extremely helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. So really my question is: As a member of the operations staff, do you know what Osmanovic, Mr. Osmanovic, was talking about when he referred to "two staffs"? And if you don't know, then don't worry.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is -- or there may be an explanation in the text itself, I don't know. But it says "the civilian protection staff." If that is a correct translation, because I don't know if it is a correct translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I see is "civilian protection," not "civilian protection staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I have in English here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you aware of a civilian protection staff, Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I even knew the president of the staff. I believe his last name was Halilovic, or something or other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Jones, I mean, I'm -- I find myself comforted in what I'm thinking by looking again at the entire -- the first part, which says, "The meeting was called to order by Osman Osmanovic. He said we were faced with problems in the functioning of the system." And there you have a colon, and you see it, "the War Presidency, two staffs, civilian protection." And then later on, further down, you see "the civilian protection staff as part of the Secretariat for National Defence. The staff is also the supreme command of the units." So I think what was bothering or -- what was in Mr. Osmanovic's mind at the time - I think, I mean, I stand to be corrected, obviously - were precisely these two staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, I think, because we probably with this witness will be entering into the realms of speculation, I'll turn to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And you have six minutes, because we'll have to stop at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to revisit, just briefly, a couple of issues concerning the food crisis in Srebrenica, and sorry if it's -- if it seems a bit of a jump, but there are a couple of matters I still need to clarify. Now, in Srebrenica, isn't it right that, because there wasn't enough flour, people were making bread from corn husks and that sort of thing, bread surrogates?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a surrogate of bread. I wouldn't really call it bread. And you would make it from corn stalks. You would take the corn off and then use the corn stalks. And then they were also using another type of a tree which had some sort of an outgrowth which was like buds, and then you would pick those and make flour out of those and then bake bread. That's what people ate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'd just like to look at another passage in War Hospital. It's pages 113 to 114, and it's describing the situation in early January 1993, and I'll read it: "Serb warplanes again blast Srebrenica, in violation of the no-fly zone declared by the United Nations. With no new aid supplies, no new offensives for the hapsi to collect food, and thousands of new refugees, food supplies vanish. People, especially those displaced from their homes in the villages, turned to old war recipes, pounding flour out of corncobs, tree buds, and the pulp of apples and pears. The diet constipates, but the doctors have no laxatives to offer." My question really was the public health issue generated by people eating this improvised bread. Is it right that it was pretty indigestible?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had several cases of ileitis, that is when the intestines get entangled, and one of the young girls there died as a result of this condition. That's when the human diet starts involving something that cannot be digested, like twigs or branches, because this was no normal diet, really. This cannot be considered as food, it had no nutritional value.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: People got pretty sick, having to eat this stuff.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases where a surgical intervention was possible, but they were undernourished due to inadequate food, diets, lack of vitamins and minerals and so on, which made them liable to pneumonia, different kinds of ailments. So when I said that people were dying of starvation, I also meant that they were dying as a result of a number of ailments resulting from undernourishment. We had premises that were not located in the hospital but in Crni Rijeka - that's a neighbourhood in the town - where we put up these patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there also a public health crisis caused by the lack of a clean water supply?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about water, whether there was shortage of clean water or not, because we didn't have the possibilities to verify the quality of water. But I'm sure that the quality was below the acceptable one. But since we never tested water at the sources, people simply drank the water that they had available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Weren't you aware at a certain point that there was a risk of an epidemic breaking out because of the lack of a clean water supply?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was always a lurking danger and risk of epidemics and outbreaks of infectious diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, on the public health issues, isn't it right that the hospital where you worked was rife with lice, that many, many of the patients had lice?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the things that we received in aid was the substance necessary for the prevention of lice infestation. But that's one of the things that seems to be a -- accompany war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think, given the time, I can stop there, and I hope to be finished by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. We will continue on Monday, Monday, as you know, we are sitting in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are sitting in the afternoon. I think the entire week is in the afternoon, if I remember well. Correct me, Mr. Siller, if I am wrong, but I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, shouldn't it be, on the Thursday, if I may, and the Friday that those are the morning sessions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could be, could be, could be. But I am certain, I am sure, that we start with the afternoon, with an afternoon for sure. Okay. Have a nice weekend. In the meantime, take every opportunity to rest, Mr. Mujkanovic, because we're still not over with your testimony. I think there are a few days more, I would expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For my part, I plan to be finished by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Monday. And then I am sure there will be a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I certainly can assure you that there will be interventions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we may be talking of an extra -- of another two days, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a matter for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.
